title: Why the SNB saw easier monetary conditions as Swiss bond yields rose
summary: A central bank can judge monetary conditions to have eased even as its government bond yields rise. That was the Swiss National Bank’s assessment when its Governing Board met on 22 and 23 September. Since the June assessment, the franc had fallen about 3% in trade-weighted terms, while Swiss interest rates had risen slightly. The Board judged the currency move more important. It held the policy rate at 0% and saw no further need for the previously increased willingness to intervene in the currency market. The option to intervene when needed remained. This account was published on 22 October, four weeks after the 24 September rate announcement. Its explanation of the decision belongs on the October publication date in any study of what investors could know at the time (summary, pp. 1–2, 6).

The currency discussion identifies a mechanism that the public decision did not quantify. Wider interest-rate differences between Switzerland and other economies increased the appeal of borrowing francs to fund investments in higher-yielding currencies. Low exchange-rate volatility made that strategy more attractive, and the SNB had seen little safe-haven demand for the franc since June. This was the Board’s assessment of the incentives for a carry trade. It provided no estimate of positions, leverage or flows. It follows that a market participant could test the argument by comparing the rate differential and currency volatility with franc returns, but could not infer the size of speculative positions from the 3% depreciation alone (‘Financial markets’, p. 2).

Other markets did not move together. The Swiss Confederation yield curve shifted up, domestic stock prices remained close to June levels and residential property prices continued to rise. Broad money growth slowed, while lending growth barely changed. Stronger global interest rates reflected several possible influences, including expectations of monetary tightening abroad, resilient activity, uncertainty over foreign fiscal policy and borrowing by AI-related businesses. Energy and US technology equities held up on corporate results despite higher global rates. These observations argue for examining local rates, currency exposure and credit separately. The rise in a Swiss ten-year yield need not have represented either an imminent change in the SNB policy rate or a tighter overall stance (‘Financial markets’ and ‘Monetary indicators’, p. 2).

The consumer-price discussion also distinguishes two different forms of pass-through. Imported oil products accounted for much of the increase that left August CPI inflation at 0.8%. Charges for inpatient hospital services also contributed that month, and the SNB’s trimmed-mean measure, TM15, rose slightly to 0.6%. Over the year so far, the behaviour of goods and services prices had broadly resembled their respective long-term averages. The Board saw little evidence of second-round effects, while recognising that longer-lasting expensive oil would increase their risk. Capacity utilisation, business costs and the ability of companies to raise selling prices would determine how much of the shock spread. A hospital charge, a fuel surcharge and a general repricing of labour-intensive services can all increase the same monthly index while conveying different information about persistent inflation (domestic price discussion, pp. 4–5).

Company interviews supplied a direct check on this mechanism. Firms anticipated higher purchase prices and a somewhat smaller increase in their own selling prices. Costs included oil-based inputs and software and cloud fees. Delivery times had lengthened somewhat, but businesses did not report disruption on the scale experienced during the pandemic. The delegates attributed variation in petrol and diesel pass-through at filling stations partly to operators’ purchasing arrangements and local competition. Companies’ short-term inflation expectations were slightly lower, medium-term expectations unchanged and expected wage increases moderate. The evidence suggested incomplete or delayed pass-through. It did not supply a single coefficient applicable to all retail prices (reports from regional delegates, pp. 3–4).

Switzerland’s activity figures made it particularly important to distinguish industry performance from economy-wide capacity. The exceptional second-quarter GDP increase included unusually strong chemicals and pharmaceutical output. Growth outside that effect was still solid. The upward revision to projected 2026 growth, to 1.5%–2%, also reflected revised 2025 data and the weaker franc. The 2027 projection remained around 1.5%. Firms reported stronger manufacturing turnover, resilient services and full construction order books, but watchmakers and some automotive suppliers remained weak. Manufacturing utilisation had improved and still lay below average. Successful exporters could coexist with considerable unused capacity in other industries (regional evidence and Swiss outlook, pp. 4–5).

The labour-market signals likewise required more than one metric. Both employment and unemployment had risen. The Board observed that unemployment in some service activities, including IT and finance, seemed higher than the economic backdrop alone might suggest. It discussed whether increased AI use could eventually have structural employment and consumption effects but did not establish a causal link. Globally, it also saw a possible productivity benefit from AI investment. For interpreting Swiss demand, the concrete starting points were mixed labour indicators and moderate company wage plans. Either a productivity boom or technology-driven structural job losses remained a hypothesis (international outlook and domestic labour discussion, pp. 3, 5–6).

The published record therefore supports three distinct judgements. Interest-rate differentials and low volatility helped explain why the franc softened. That depreciation more than offset a modest increase in rates in the Board’s assessment of monetary conditions. And stronger imported prices had so far produced little evidence of a domestic inflation feedback. The SNB accordingly regarded current conditions as sufficient for medium-term price stability. A market study should distinguish the earlier movements described by the Board from the reaction to its decision in September and the incremental information in this October account. None of the three intervals measures the others (monetary indicators and final decision, pp. 2, 6).

questions.question: Did the currency adjustment ease Swiss financial conditions by more than higher interest rates tightened them?
questions.detail: Compare effective franc moves with changes in Confederation yields, corporate borrowing costs and new lending terms between the June and September assessments. Then examine input prices and exporters’ order books by currency exposure. The Board supplied the sign of the combined effect but no estimated weights or exchange-rate elasticity.

questions.question: Was the franc decline driven by carry incentives, and what could reverse it?
questions.detail: Track Swiss–foreign short-rate differentials, implied volatility, option skew and safe-haven episodes together. A change in cross-currency positioning would need independent position or flow data. The summary links depreciation to incentives while leaving open how quickly renewed risk aversion could outweigh them.

questions.question: Where were firms able to pass procurement costs on to customers?
questions.detail: Compare reported input and selling-price intentions with subsequent realised prices, sector utilisation and competitive conditions. Distinguish petroleum, software fees and healthcare charges from wage-sensitive domestic services. Persistent rises in the trimmed-mean measure alongside wage settlements would carry different policy implications from another fuel-price adjustment.

questions.question: How much of the 2026 growth upgrade could be repeated?
questions.detail: Separate volatile pharmaceutical exports and revisions to the prior year from broad domestic turnover, hiring and real consumption. Compare the subsequent figures to the publication vintage. If strong output was concentrated in export timing while utilisation stayed soft, Swiss rate and currency exposures could diverge more than the headline growth rate suggested.
